turns.doctor_question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I... I came in because, well, it’s been going on for a while now, and I just can't shake it, no matter how much I try to rationalize it. I work as a personal financial advisor, right? And I have a lot of clients, a lot of connections, especially in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati. It’s a tight-knit group, you know, everyone knows everyone, or at least they know of everyone. But lately, or I guess for a few months now, I’ve been absolutely convinced that certain people—specific people in these circles—are quietly tracking me. Tracking who I meet with, which clients I’m taking on, where I’m going. 

And it’s not just that they’re watching, it’s how they’re doing it. They’re sending me these... little signals. It sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but it’s in the details. Like, I’ll get an invitation to a gallery opening or a networking dinner, and the wording on the invite, or the specific panel topics they choose to discuss—it’s too specific to what I’ve been working on. And then at these events, it’s who sits near me. It’s always someone connected to a deal I’m looking at or a client I just met with. I keep telling myself, "Come on, it’s just a coincidence, Cincinnati isn't that big, it’s just how networking works." I try to brush it off. But I can’t. I just can’t let it go. It’s like this constant hum in the back of my mind, analyzing every interaction, every seating arrangement, every email subject line. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to figure out what they’re trying to tell me or why they’re keeping tabs on me like this.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, persistent belief that people are tracking them and sending hidden signals through everyday occurrences like invitations and seating arrangements, which they cannot shake despite attempts to rationalize.

It's a smaller pond. You're going to see the same fish." And I really do try to lean into that. I'll sit there at my desk, looking at an email invite to a gallery opening in Over-the-Rhine, and I'll see that the featured artist just happens to be doing a series on, I don't know, urban decay, which exactly mirrors a real estate development deal I was just discussing in private with a client the day before. And I'll say to myself, "It's just a coincidence. It's just the zeitgeist." 

But then... I go to the event. And the person they seat next to me at the dinner afterward is the lead investor on a competing project. And the centerpieces are arranged in a way that... well, it just feels too deliberate. So, do I believe it for certain? I don't want to. I really, really don't want to. I try to talk myself out of it constantly. But the feeling, the absolute conviction that they are keeping tabs on me, that they are coordinating these little signals to let me know they're watching my moves... it just overpowers the logic. I can't shake it. No matter how much I tell myself it's crazy, I'm still absolutely convinced it's happening. It's like a weight I can't put down, just constantly analyzing the overlap, the connections, the sheer impossibility of it all being random chance. So, yes, despite my best efforts to rationalize it away, I am convinced they are tracking me.

turns.doctor_question: Do these thoughts about people tracking you feel intrusive and unwanted, like thoughts you know are probably not true but can’t stop, or do they feel like a real fact about what’s happening?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that’s... I mean, I really want it to be the first one. I really, really want it to just be my brain playing tricks on me, like some sort of weird stress response. Because in my line of work—being a financial advisor—you are literally trained to look for patterns, right? You look at market indicators, you analyze historical data, and you project forward. It’s all about finding the signal in the noise. So for a long time, I tried to convince myself that my brain was just stuck in that mode, just... over-applying my professional pattern recognition to my social life, to these arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati. 

I’d sit there and think, "Okay, this is just an unwanted thought. You're just stressed about your portfolio." But... the problem is, it doesn't stay in my head. It doesn't feel like just a thought, because the evidence is physical. It feels like a completely real fact about what is actually happening in the world around me. 

Because I can hold the invitations in my hand, you know? I can look at the printed agenda for a networking dinner and see the specific panel topics they’ve chosen, and I can see exactly how it aligns with the private meetings I just had. I can walk into a room and see the seating chart, and see exactly who they’ve placed next to me. It’s not just a passing worry. I am convinced that they are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. The signals they are sending me are real, tangible things. 

And even when I desperately tell myself, "Hey, maybe it's just a coincidence, maybe the event planner just sat us together randomly because we're in similar industries," I just... I can’t really let it go. I can't. Because the math just doesn't add up for it to be random chance every single time. I mean, if you look at the statistical probability of the exact same people from the exact same competing firms being seated next to me at three different charity galas in a single quarter, right after I’ve taken on a major new client... the odds are astronomical! 

So, yes, it feels like a real fact. It feels like I've stumbled onto this coordinated effort to keep tabs on me. And it’s incredibly frustrating because I’m a logical guy, I have my degree, I manage millions of dollars for people, and I know exactly how it sounds to say "they're sending me signals." But when you're living it, when you see the actual paper trail of the invites and the seating charts and the perfectly timed conversations, it stops being just some thought you can push away. It becomes the reality you have to navigate every single day. I just keep trying to explain it away to myself, and I just end up right back at the absolute fact that it is actually happening.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient firmly believes they are being tracked and sent signals, stating it feels like a 'completely real fact' and an 'absolute fact that it is actually happening,' despite trying to explain it away.
symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly rejects the idea that these are just intrusive, unwanted thoughts they know are untrue, stating instead that they feel like real facts.

It feels like a lifetime. I’ve even started color-coding my digital calendar to track the anomalies over this two-month period—red for a direct signal, yellow for a suspected one—and the concentration of it all is just overwhelming. It all started right after that big push for new clients, and it just hasn't let up for a single week since.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, two-month-long belief that people are tracking his confidential meetings and sending him specific signals, indicating persecutory and referential delusions.

Well, no, I wouldn't call it sudden. And honestly, it wasn't really a stressful event that kicked it all off, either. I mean, not in a negative way, at least. This gradual accumulation of oddities and subtle signals ever since that night two years ago. 

I can still picture the exact venue, standing by the bar and thinking, "Why is everyone suddenly so intensely interested in my proprietary data?" And it just grew from there, inch by inch, quarter by quarter. So, no, not a sudden stressor. Just a very long, very drawn-out escalation that started the night they handed me that glass plaque.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a two-year build-up of absolute certainty that people are tracking him and sending subtle signals about his proprietary data, indicating referential and persecutory delusions.
